title: Beam Deflection vs Cross Section
prompt: A rectangular cantilever beam (width b, thickness h in the bending direction) carries a fixed tip load. By what factor does tip deflection change if (a) the thickness h is halved, (b) the width b is halved?
solution:
Deflection δ ∝ 1/(E·I), with I = b·h³/12.
(a) h → h/2: I drops by 2³ = 8, so δ is 8× larger.
(b) b → b/2: I halves, so δ is 2× larger.
Depth is the cheap way to buy stiffness, which is why beams are tall and thin and I-beams put material far from the neutral axis.

title: Pressure Vessel Principal Stresses
prompt: A closed thin-walled cylinder has radius 0.5 m, wall thickness 3 mm, and internal pressure 1.0 MPa. Find the hoop stress, the axial stress, the maximum in-plane shear stress, and the absolute maximum shear stress (treat radial stress at the outer wall as ≈ 0).
answer: σ_hoop = 167 MPa, σ_axial = 83 MPa, τ_in-plane = 42 MPa, τ_abs = 83 MPa
solution:
σ_hoop = Pr/t = 1.0 × 500 / 3 = 166.7 MPa
σ_axial = Pr/2t = 83.3 MPa
In-plane Mohr's circle: τ_max = (σ1 − σ2)/2 = (166.7 − 83.3)/2 = 41.7 MPa
The three principal stresses are hoop, axial and radial (≈ 0 outside, −P inside), so the largest circle spans hoop to radial: τ_abs = 166.7/2 = 83.3 MPa.
Hoop stress is twice axial, which is why cylinders split lengthwise.

title: Stress-Strain: Ductile vs Brittle
prompt: Sketch a stress-strain curve with real numbers for a ductile material and a brittle one. Explain the key regions and points, and how cracks propagate differently in each.
solution: Ductile (mild/structural steel): linear elastic with slope E ≈ 200 GPa up to yield, about 460 MPa by the 0.2% offset. Then strain hardening to UTS of about 560 MPa at around 10% strain, then necking and fracture at about 20% elongation. Brittle (cast iron, ceramics, glass): nearly linear right up to fracture, with no yield or necking and under about 1% strain to failure. Cracks: stress concentrates at the crack tip, K = Yσ√(πa), and fast fracture happens when K reaches the fracture toughness K_IC. In a ductile metal a plastic zone blunts the tip and absorbs energy, so cracks grow slowly and stably, often by fatigue (Paris law). In a brittle material there's no blunting, so once K_IC is reached the crack runs unstably.
keyPoints: Elastic slope E; steel ≈ 200 GPa
Yield by 0.2% offset; UTS; necking; elongation at break
Brittle: linear to fracture, small strain, no yield
Stress intensity K = Yσ√(πa) vs fracture toughness K_IC
Ductile tip blunting and plastic zone vs unstable brittle fracture
Fatigue crack growth (Paris law) as the common real failure

title: Thermal Diffusivity
prompt: What is thermal diffusivity, how is it defined, and what does a high value mean physically? Compare copper and 304 stainless.
answer: α = k/(ρ·c_p): how fast temperature changes spread through a material
solution: α = k/(ρc_p) is heat conducted divided by heat stored, in m²/s. A high α means a temperature change at the surface reaches the interior quickly, so the material equalizes fast. Copper: 401/(8960 × 385) ≈ 1.2×10⁻⁴ m²/s. 304 SS: 16.2/(8000 × 500) ≈ 4×10⁻⁶ m²/s, about 30× slower. That's why copper liners spread throat heat into the coolant and why stainless heats up locally during welding.

title: Radiating Nozzle Extension
prompt: A radiatively cooled nozzle extension has 1.0 m² of outer surface at 1500 K with emissivity 0.8, radiating to deep space (take the surroundings as 0 K). How much heat does it reject, in kW? Also state the governing equations for conduction, convection and radiation.
solution:
Radiation: Q = εσA(T₂⁴ − T₁⁴) = 0.8 × 5.67×10⁻⁸ × 1 × 1500⁴ ≈ 229.7 kW.
Conduction: Q = kA·ΔT/L. Convection: Q = hA·ΔT. Sensible heat absorbed: Q = m·c_p·ΔT.
Because of the T⁴ term, radiation only matters at high temperature, which is why radiatively cooled extensions run red hot (niobium, carbon-carbon).

title: Bernoulli Through a Contraction
prompt: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows at 3 m/s in a 50 mm line that contracts to 25 mm. Assuming ideal, level, incompressible flow, what is the pressure drop across the contraction, in kPa?
solution:
Continuity: V₁A₁ = V₂A₂. Halving the diameter quarters the area, so V₂ = 12 m/s.
Bernoulli: ΔP = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = 0.5 × 1000 × (144 − 9) = 67,500 Pa = 67.5 kPa.
The general steady-flow energy equation, Q − W = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz], reduces to Bernoulli when there's no heat, no work and no losses.

title: What Is a Boundary Layer, Exactly
prompt: What is a boundary layer, exactly? Describe the velocity and thermal boundary layers and how the Prandtl number relates them.
solution: It's the thin region near a wall where viscosity matters. No-slip makes velocity zero at the wall, rising to 99% of free-stream velocity at the edge, which defines the thickness δ. It grows along the surface and transitions from laminar to turbulent. The thermal boundary layer is the analogous region where temperature goes from T_wall to 99% of T_∞. Pr = ν/α compares momentum diffusion to heat diffusion. At Pr = 1 the two layers are the same thickness. At Pr ≫ 1 (oils, kerosene) the velocity layer is much thicker. At Pr ≪ 1 (liquid metals) the thermal layer is much thicker. Nearly all the resistance to convective heat transfer sits in this layer.
keyPoints: No-slip wall; 99% of free-stream velocity defines thickness
Grows downstream; laminar to turbulent transition
Thermal BL: 99% of free-stream temperature
Pr = ν/α sets relative thickness of the two layers
BL is where the convective heat-transfer resistance lives

title: Prandtl Number and h
prompt: Define the Prandtl number and give typical values for water, LOX, kerosene, air and liquid metals. If a higher Pr gives a higher Nusselt number, does it always give a higher heat transfer coefficient h?
answer: Pr = ν/α = μc_p/k. No: h = Nu·k/L, so a low-k fluid can have high Nu but low h.
solution: Pr = ν/α = μc_p/k. Typical values: water ≈ 7 at room temperature, LOX ≈ 2 at saturation, kerosene ≈ 15, air ≈ 0.7, liquid metals ≈ 0.001–0.01. Correlations give Nu ∝ Reᵐ·Prⁿ, so higher Pr raises Nu, but h = Nu·k/L. High-Pr fluids are usually high-Pr because k is low, so h isn't necessarily higher.

title: Reynolds Number in a LOX Line
prompt: LOX (ρ = 1141 kg/m³, μ = 1.9×10⁻⁴ Pa·s) flows at 5 m/s through a 100 mm diameter line. What is the Reynolds number, and is the flow laminar or turbulent?
solution:
Re = ρVD/μ = 1141 × 5 × 0.1 / 1.9×10⁻⁴ ≈ 3.0×10⁶.
Re is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. Pipe flow transitions at Re ≈ 2300 and is fully turbulent above about 4000, so this is deep in turbulence. Low-viscosity cryogens are almost always turbulent in feed lines.

title: Nusselt Number
prompt: What does the Nusselt number represent, and what does Nu = 1 mean?
answer: Nu = hL/k: convective vs conductive heat transfer across the fluid. Nu = 1 is pure conduction.
solution: Nu = hL/k compares how well a moving fluid carries heat away from a surface to what conduction alone through a stagnant layer of the same fluid would do. Nu = 1 means no convective enhancement (pure conduction). Turbulent flows reach hundreds to thousands. You get h back from a correlation: h = Nu·k/L.

title: Stagnation vs Static Temperature
prompt: Air (c_p = 1005 J/kg·K) at a static temperature of 300 K moves at 500 m/s. What is its stagnation temperature, in K? Explain stagnation vs static pressure and temperature.
solution:
T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p) = 300 + 500²/(2 × 1005) ≈ 424.4 K.
Static values are what you'd measure moving with the flow, without its kinetic energy. Stagnation (total) values are what you'd get if the flow were brought to rest: adiabatically for T₀, isentropically for P₀. Incompressible: P₀ = P + ½ρV². This is why a probe facing into fast flow reads hot and high.

title: Natural Convection in Space
prompt: Why does natural convection fail in space?
answer: It's driven by buoyancy, which needs gravity. In microgravity there's no buoyant force, and in vacuum there's no fluid at all.
solution: Natural convection happens because hot fluid is less dense and gravity makes it rise (buoyancy ∝ ρgβΔT, the Grashof number). In orbit, effective g ≈ 0, so warm fluid doesn't rise and only conduction is left. Outside the spacecraft there's no medium, leaving radiation. Spacecraft use fans, pumped loops and radiators instead.

title: Enthalpy Through Thermo Cycles
prompt: Explain enthalpy, and walk through how it changes across the components of some common thermodynamic cycles.
solution: Enthalpy h = u + Pv is internal energy plus flow work, the energy a flowing stream carries. For steady flow, Q − W = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz], so in an adiabatic turbine or pump the work equals Δh. Rankine: the pump raises h slightly, the boiler raises h a lot at constant P, the turbine drops h to make work, and the condenser drops h to reject heat. Brayton: the compressor raises h, the combustor raises h, and the turbine drops h, with the leftover enthalpy driving the nozzle. A throttling valve is isenthalpic (h constant, P and often T drop). A rocket nozzle turns chamber enthalpy into kinetic energy: V_e = √(2(h₀ − h_e)).
keyPoints: h = u + Pv; energy carried by a flowing stream
Steady-flow energy equation: adiabatic work = Δh
Rankine: pump ↑ small, boiler ↑, turbine ↓, condenser ↓
Brayton: compressor ↑, combustor ↑, turbine ↓
Throttle is isenthalpic
Nozzle converts enthalpy to velocity

title: Spring-Mass Natural Frequency
prompt: Starting from F = ma and F = −kx, derive the natural frequency of a spring-mass system. Then compute it for m = 10 kg and k = 40 kN/m, in Hz.
solution:
ma = −kx gives ẍ + (k/m)x = 0: simple harmonic motion with ωₙ = √(k/m).
ωₙ = √(40000/10) = 63.2 rad/s, so fₙ = ωₙ/2π ≈ 10.07 Hz.
The rotational analog is T = Iα with torsional stiffness: ωₙ = √(k_t/I). Stiffer means higher frequency and more mass means lower, which is the basis for detuning modes like pogo.

title: Hardest Technical Project
prompt: What is the hardest technical project you've done?
solution: There's no model answer for this one: prepare your own story and practice telling it in about 2 minutes. Structure: the problem and why it was hard, in technical terms with real numbers; what you personally owned and decided ("I", not "we"); the key engineering tradeoff or failure and how you debugged it from first principles; the result, measured; and what you'd do differently. Expect follow-ups drilling into any number or decision you mention, so pick a project you can defend down to the hand calcs.
keyPoints: Hard for a technical reason, stated with numbers
Your personal ownership and decisions
A failure or tradeoff and how you worked through it
Measured result
Lessons learned; can defend every detail

title: Heated Washer and Thermal Stress
prompt: A steel washer has ID 20 mm and OD 40 mm. It is heated uniformly and the OD grows to 40.8 mm (×1.02). (a) What is the new ID? (b) Now suppose instead the inner edge is hot and the outer edge stays cold. Describe the stress state.
solution:
(a) Uniform heating scales every dimension by the same 1 + αΔT, holes included: ID = 20 × 1.02 = 20.4 mm. The hole behaves like the missing material would. (For steel, 2% would take ΔT ≈ 1670 K, so it's purely illustrative.)
(b) The hot inner region wants to grow but the cold rim holds it back. The inner region is in hoop compression, the cold outer rim is stretched into hoop tension, and radial stress is compressive in between and zero at the free ID and OD. Cracks start at the cold, tensile outer edge, which is why hot-centered glass and brake discs crack from the rim.
